line: Welcome. Guo. I run the Saturday school and the festival committee. Dr. Zhou chairs the board these days. Is this your first time in?
choice1: Yes. I'm {playerName}, I live on Grand.
choice3: I'm not really looking for an association, thanks.

line: Good. The noticeboard is by the door. Saturday school, seniors' lunch Tuesdays and Saturdays, the Mid-Autumn festival in September. Did someone send you, or did you find us?
choice1: My mother told me about it.
choice3: I'll have a look at the board. Thanks.

line: Then she raised you well. Most parents now let the children decide, and the children decide on the mall.
choice1: How long has the center been here?
choice2: I'll look around. Nice to meet you.

line: That's unusual, for your generation. Usually somebody has to bring them in by the sleeve. Usually a grandmother.
choice1: How long has the center been here?
choice2: I'll look around. Nice to meet you.

line: The Saturday school, forty-one years. This building, twenty-six. We bought it with dinners, raffles, and three families who put up their savings. No grants.
Grants come with a man from the city who wants a report. Then the money moves to the next neighbourhood, and the report stays. What we pay for ourselves, nobody can take away.

In 2009 the city paid for an English class here. Two years, a very good teacher. Then the budget changed, and one Tuesday forty students were standing in my hallway asking me where she went. $ [neutral] I didn't have an answer. I don't like not having an answer.
Anyway. Come on Saturday. We always need someone who can lift tables.
choice2: Maybe. Nice to meet you, Mr. Guo.

line: No. _hands behind his back_ Old Wu walks past the tables and reports. He says Lin is losing on purpose. He thinks nobody can see.
choice2: I'll let you finish your lap.

line: Old Wu says he keeps his horse at home so Walt can feel clever. Thirty years Lin and I argue about everything. The one thing we agree on: never tell Walt.
choice1: Your secret's safe. Do you play?

line: Here, Thursdays, with Lin and Old Wu, at the back table. In the park the game is for the people walking past.
It's a good park. Everyone is friendly, and in a year nobody there will know your name. Here they know it the second time.
choice1: I'll come on a Thursday, then.

line: Two laps of the courtyard out back after lunch, then the office. My wife times me. If I come back early she sends me out again.
If you can keep up. _sets off round the courtyard at a steady pace_ You know the park on Grand? With the chess tables?
Lin plays there every morning, with Walt. I told him Walt will never learn the real game. He says that's not the point.
choice2: Do you ever go and watch?
choice3: I'll let you finish your lap.

line: Lin says a friend. I say he has friends at the center. He says, different friends. _keeps walking_ Lin was always the softer one.
Not bad. But when Lin's wife was in hospital, it was the center that cooked for a month. Walt sent a card. A nice card.
Ah, you. The Mid-Autumn committee needs people who can lift tables and also read a spreadsheet. It's a rare combination.
Good. Thursday, seven. Mrs. Ho does the spreadsheet, and she does not like help. You'll start with the tables.
Two hundred lanterns. The lion dance team from the Saturday school. Mooncakes ordered in July, so the bakery doesn't run out. Last year eight hundred people.
choice2: That's a lot of lanterns. See you Thursday.

line: Families from here, mostly. Some from outside, who take photographs. A newspaper came once and wrote the word 'exotic.' We did not invite them again.
Ah. Sit a minute. I want to ask you something.
Ah. Sit a minute. I want to ask you something.
Dr. Zhou wants us to do a forum with the library. The city says partner, partner. I have to decide what goes to the board. What do you think?
choice3: I'd have to think about it.

line: Dr. Zhou has her forum with the library. The board voted five to two. I was one of the two. What do you think?
choice1: It sounds like a good idea.
choice3: I'd have to think about it.

line: I think, when the money stops, who is still here? Us. Ruth Hale is a decent woman, I've met her. She will retire, and the next one will not know our name.
choice3: I'll let you think it over.

line: Maybe not. But I've seen it go that way. First you share a room, then you share a budget, then the young ones decide the other room is nicer. $ [warm] I'm not against the library. I just want this place open when the Saturday school children are my age.
Good, you're here. The festival committee has dinner at my house on Sunday.
Only the core people. I want you there. My wife is making red-braised pork, so skip lunch.
Mrs. Ho, the treasurer. Lin, who will complain about the pork. Dr. Zhou, if she isn't at the hospital. We argue, we eat, and at the end Mrs. Ho decides.
You know what I like about the courtyard out back? Nobody out there wants anything from me. In here everyone has a question before I take off my coat.
Hm. _almost smiles_ My wife says the same. Twenty-six years I've had the keys to this building. When I'm sick, I lie in bed and wonder who opened it.
That's the question. Mrs. Ho is seventy. The young ones come for the lunch and go home. One or two might stay.
choice1: Would you let them change things?

line: A little. Not the Saturday school. Not the lunch. The lanterns, they can do however they like. Lin says I'll say that and then complain about the lanterns.
Good afternoon. You've seen the news.

People have been coming in since Monday, asking what to do. Mostly old people, with papers that are perfectly fine. $ [neutral] I'm not surprised. Every few years Washington needs somebody to point at, and we are easy to point at.
We keep a lawyer's number on the board. Ms. Tan comes the first Saturday of the month. Washington changes its mind every four years. The association is still here.
choice1: Can the association handle it alone?

line: Not everything. But Ms. Tan's mother sent her to my Saturday school. When the lawyer knows your mother, you tell her the truth. The city office doesn't get the truth.
Good afternoon. Everyone is excited about the new president.
Mrs. Ho cried at the television. I'm glad for her. Fine.
In four years, someone else. The Saturday school has been here forty-one years. It was here under six presidents.
choice2: Forty-one years is a long time.
choice3: Then why do you think he won?

line: Maybe. If he helps, good, we'll use it. But I won't move the school into a program that ends when he does. I've seen that before.

Because people voted together. Last spring we registered four hundred people in this building, between the soup and the oranges. The Korean church did the same, the Vietnamese association too. $ He didn't come to us. We came to him, in a block, and he can count.
choice2: Lots of people voted for him.

line: That's power, here. Not a program from the city. Four hundred names on a list I can call. Keep the list long, and whoever sits in Washington has to listen. $ So. Come Thursday. We need people who stay.
Ah, the library regular. Dr. Zhou tells me you go to Ruth Hale's potlucks.
choice2: I still come here, Mr. Guo.

line: Ah, the library regular. Dr. Zhou tells me you go to Ruth Hale's potlucks. She was delighted. I said, we'll see.
choice2: I still come here, Mr. Guo.

line: I hope so. What do they serve?
Hm. And do they ask you about here?
They ask once, and then they ask about the food. _not unkindly_ Come on a Saturday. The lunch is not a casserole, and nobody will ask you to explain it.
You're here so often I keep forgetting you're not on the committee.
Thursdays. It's not glamorous. Tables, lanterns, Mrs. Ho's spreadsheet.
choice1: Why does it matter so much to you?

line: When I came, nobody knew my name except the man who rented me a room over his restaurant. Then I found the Saturday school, and an old teacher there found me a job.
Forty-four years. I've been paying her back the whole time. She died in 2003. The school doesn't know that's what it is. You do now.
Hm. You came back.
choice1: I spoke out of turn before. I'm sorry.

line: Hm. Accepted. Young people are allowed to say what they think. Once.
Not now. My wife is expecting me, and she times me.
